etymology: Hebrew Hadoram (H1913), commonly read Hadar is exalted, the first element being the name of a Syrian deity; the man who served Rehoboam is called Adoram in Kings and Adoniram in the record of Solomon's levy.
biblical_def: Three men bear this name. The first is a son of Joktan in the table of nations, one of the Arabian peoples descended from Shem (Gen 10:27; 1Ch 1:21). The second is a son of Tou king of Hamath, sent to David with vessels of gold and silver and brass to congratulate him on defeating Hadarezer, the common enemy of both (1Ch 18:10). The third is the officer who was over the tribute under Rehoboam, called Adoram in Kings, and his end is one of the sharpest scenes in the history of the divided kingdom. Rehoboam, having answered Israel's plea for a lighter yoke with a threat of scorpions, sent the tax collector to enforce it, and all Israel stoned him with stones, that he died. Therefore king Rehoboam made speed to get him up to his chariot, to flee to Jerusalem (1Ki 12:18). The man had served Solomon over the levy and Rehoboam over the tribute, and the king sent him into a city that had just renounced the crown. He was stoned for a policy he did not make, by people whose complaint was just, at the order of a king who then ran.
webster_summary: The name of three men: a son of Joktan, a son of Tou king of Hamath, and Rehoboam's officer over the tribute, who was stoned by Israel.
webster_full: HADORAM, Hebrew Hadoram, commonly read Hadar is exalted.
1. A son of Joktan in the table of the nations, of the sons of Shem.
2. A son of Tou king of Hamath, sent with gifts to congratulate David.
3. The officer over the tribute under Rehoboam; called Adoram in the book of Kings.
All Israel stoned him with stones, and Rehoboam fled to Jerusalem in his chariot.
scriptures: And Hadoram, and Uzal, and Diklah,
Hadoram also, and Uzal, and Diklah,
Then king Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was over the tribute; and all Israel stoned him with stones, that he died. Therefore king Rehoboam made speed to get him up to his chariot, to flee to Jerusalem.
And Adoram was over the tribute: and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder:
corruption_summary: Leaders are judged by their intentions and their subordinates by their outcomes; Scripture puts the cost of Rehoboam's folly on the man he sent.
corruption_paragraphs: The stoning of Adoram is the bill for Rehoboam's speech. The old men had counselled the king to speak good words to the people and they would be his servants for ever; the young men who had grown up with him advised the threat of scorpions; he took the second counsel, the ten tribes departed, and then he sent the tax officer into the breach. The man who died was the man who had been doing that job since Solomon's day. Rehoboam kept his chariot.

Scripture is unsentimental about the weight of office. My brethren, be not many masters, knowing that we shall receive the greater condemnation (Jas 3:1); the shepherd who flees when he sees the wolf coming is named a hireling because the sheep are not his (Joh 10:12-13); and the Good Shepherd is known by the opposite motion — He giveth His life for the sheep. The principle to recover is that authority is measured by who absorbs the cost when a decision goes wrong. A leader whose errors are paid for by the people under him has not led them; he has spent them.
roots_summary: Hebrew Hadoram (H1913); the same officer appears as Adoram (H151) and Adoniram (H141), my lord is exalted.
roots_lines: Hebrew Hadoram (H1913) — a son of Joktan (Gen 10:27), a son of Tou (1Ch 18:10), and Rehoboam's officer (2Ch 10:18).
Hebrew Adoram (H151) — the form used in 2 Samuel 20:24 and 1 Kings 12:18 for the officer over the tribute.
Hebrew mas (H4522) — tribute, forced labour, a levy; the burden Israel asked Rehoboam to lighten.
Hebrew ol (H5923) — a yoke; thy father made our yoke grievous (1Ki 12:4).
Greek misthotos (G3411) — a hireling; the hireling fleeth, because he is an hireling (Joh 10:13).
usage: “And Hadoram, and Uzal, and Diklah” — among the sons of Joktan.
“Then king Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was over the tribute”.
“King Rehoboam made speed to get him up to his chariot, to flee to Jerusalem”.

etymology: Hebrew Pelatyah (H6410), the LORD delivers or whom the LORD has caused to escape — from palat (H6403), to slip away, to deliver, to bring to safety, and Yah, the covenant name.
biblical_def: Four men bear this name, and one of them dies in the middle of a sermon. Ezekiel, carried in vision to the east gate of the LORD's house, saw five and twenty men, among whom I saw Jaazaniah the son of Azur, and Pelatiah the son of Benaiah, princes of the people (Eze 11:1). These were the men devising mischief and giving wicked counsel in the city, saying the city was the cauldron and they the flesh — secure, established, untouchable. Ezekiel was commanded to prophesy against them, and while he was still prophesying, Pelatiah the son of Benaiah died (Eze 11:13). The prophet fell on his face and cried, Ah Lord GOD! wilt thou make a full end of the remnant of Israel? The other three are a son of Hananiah in the royal line of Judah (1Ch 3:21), a captain of the Simeonites who went to mount Seir (1Ch 4:42), and a sealer of Nehemiah's covenant (Neh 10:22). The name of the prince who died means the LORD delivers — a confession of rescue, borne by a man who counted himself safe and was not.
webster_summary: The name of four men, chiefly the prince of Jerusalem who died as Ezekiel prophesied against him; it means the LORD delivers.
webster_full: PELATIAH, Hebrew Pelatyah, the LORD delivers, or whom the LORD causes to escape.
1. Pelatiah the son of Benaiah, a prince of the people seen by Ezekiel at the east gate.
He died while the prophet was yet prophesying against him.
2. A son of Hananiah, in the royal line of Judah after the captivity.
3. A captain of the Simeonites who smote the Amalekites in mount Seir. 4. A sealer of Nehemiah's covenant.
scriptures: Eze 11:1

Moreover the spirit lifted me up, and brought me unto the east gate of the LORD'S house, which looketh eastward: and behold at the door of the gate five and twenty men; among whom I saw Jaazaniah the son of Azur, and Pelatiah the son of Benaiah, princes of the people.

And it came to pass, when I prophesied, that Pelatiah the son of Benaiah died. Then fell I down upon my face, and cried with a loud voice, and said, Ah Lord GOD! wilt thou make a full end of the remnant of Israel?
And the sons of Hananiah; Pelatiah, and Jesaiah: the sons of Rephaiah, the sons of Arnan, the sons of Obadiah, the sons of Shechaniah.
And some of them, even of the sons of Simeon, five hundred men, went to mount Seir, having for their captains Pelatiah, and Neariah, and Rephaiah, and Uzziel, the sons of Ishi.
corruption_summary: Preaching is treated as commentary that costs nothing; Scripture presents the word as an instrument by which God actually acts.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 11 is intolerable to a view of preaching as religious opinion. The prophet is commanded to speak against named men who are giving wicked counsel in Jerusalem, and as he speaks one of them drops dead. Ezekiel himself is horrified by it — he falls on his face and asks whether God means to make a full end. He did not enjoy the power of the word; he was frightened by it.

Scripture never treats the preached word as inert. Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces? (Jer 23:29). It is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword (Heb 4:12), and it is the savour of death unto death to some and the savour of life unto life to others (2Co 2:16). The principle to recover is that a sermon is not a lecture with religious content; it is God addressing men, and the consequences of hearing it are real in both directions. Pelatiah bore a name that said the LORD delivers, sat among the men who said the city could not fall, and did not survive the sermon.
roots_summary: Hebrew Pelatyah (H6410), from palat (H6403), to deliver, to bring to safety, with Yah.
roots_lines: Hebrew palat (H6403) — to escape, to deliver, to carry away to safety.
Hebrew Pelatyah (H6410) — borne by four men; Ezekiel 11:1, 11:13, 1 Chronicles 3:21, 4:42, Nehemiah 10:22.
Hebrew peletah (H6413) — an escape, a remnant that gets away; the remnant that is escaped (Isa 37:32).
Hebrew sir (H5518) — a pot, a cauldron; this city is the caldron, and we be the flesh (Eze 11:3).
Greek energes (G1756) — effectual, active, at work; the word of God is quick, and powerful (Heb 4:12).
usage: “Pelatiah the son of Benaiah, princes of the people”.
“When I prophesied, that Pelatiah the son of Benaiah died”.
“Ah Lord GOD! wilt thou make a full end of the remnant of Israel?”

etymology: Hebrew Rephayah (H7509), the LORD heals — from rapha (H7495), to heal, to cure, to restore, and Yah, the covenant name; the same verb in I am the LORD that healeth thee (Exo 15:26).
biblical_def: Five men bear this name. One stands in the royal line of Judah after the captivity (1Ch 3:21); one is a captain of the Simeonites who went up to mount Seir (1Ch 4:42); one is a son of Tola of Issachar, head of a father's house among men reckoned valiant men of might in their generations (1Ch 7:2); one is a Benjamite in Saul's genealogy (1Ch 9:43); and one is Rephaiah the son of Hur, the ruler of the half part of Jerusalem, who took his place on the wall under Nehemiah (Neh 3:9). That last is the most striking. A man with civil authority over half the capital picked up a trowel and repaired his section like everyone else. Nehemiah's register names rulers, priests, goldsmiths, apothecaries, merchants and daughters, all on the same wall. The name means the LORD heals, and healing in Scripture is never merely physical: Heal me, O LORD, and I shall be healed (Jer 17:14); he healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds (Psa 147:3); and of the Servant, with his stripes we are healed (Isa 53:5).
webster_summary: The name of five men, including the ruler of half of Jerusalem who repaired a section of the wall under Nehemiah. It means the LORD heals.
webster_full: REPHAIAH, Hebrew Rephayah, the LORD heals.
1. A descendant of David in the royal line after the captivity.
2. A captain of the Simeonites who smote the Amalekites in mount Seir.
3. A son of Tola of the tribe of Issachar, head of a father's house.
4. A Benjamite in the genealogy of Saul. 5. Son of Hur, ruler of the half part of Jerusalem, who repaired the wall.
scriptures: Neh 3:9
And next unto them repaired Rephaiah the son of Hur, the ruler of the half part of Jerusalem.

And the sons of Tola; Uzzi, and Rephaiah, and Jeriel, and Jahmai, and Jibsam, and Shemuel, heads of their father's house, to wit, of Tola: they were valiant men of might in their generations; whose number was in the days of David two and twenty thousand and six hundred.
And the sons of Hananiah; Pelatiah, and Jesaiah: the sons of Rephaiah, the sons of Arnan, the sons of Obadiah, the sons of Shechaniah.
And Moza begat Binea; and Rephaiah his son, Eleasah his son, Azel his son.
corruption_summary: Healing is claimed as a right the believer may demand; Scripture makes it a mercy God gives, often deferred to the resurrection.
corruption_paragraphs: A large strand of modern teaching holds that physical healing is guaranteed in the atonement and available on demand to anyone with sufficient faith, so that continued sickness proves a defect in the sufferer. The pastoral cruelty of this is matched only by its distance from the text. Paul left Trophimus at Miletum sick (2Ti 4:20); Timothy was told to take a little wine for his stomach's sake and his often infirmities (1Ti 5:23); Epaphroditus was sick nigh unto death, and Paul ascribes his recovery to God's mercy rather than to anyone's technique (Php 2:27); and Paul's own thorn was not removed, with the answer given instead: My grace is sufficient for thee (2Co 12:9).

What Scripture does promise is that the LORD is the healer — I am the LORD that healeth thee (Exo 15:26) — that He is to be asked, and that the deepest healing is already accomplished: with his stripes we are healed, which Peter applies to the soul returning to the Shepherd (1Pe 2:24-25). The rest waits for the body's redemption, when there shall be no more pain (Rev 21:4). The principle to recover is that healing is a gift and not a lever, that every believer who has ever lived has eventually died, and that the God who has healed the worst of it may be trusted with the timing of the remainder.
roots_summary: Hebrew Rephayah (H7509), from rapha (H7495), to heal, to restore, with Yah.
roots_lines: Hebrew rapha (H7495) — to heal, to cure, to make whole; I am the LORD that healeth thee (Exo 15:26).
Hebrew Rephayah (H7509) — borne by five men; 1 Chronicles 3:21, 4:42, 7:2, 9:43, Nehemiah 3:9.
Hebrew marpe (H4832) — a cure, health, a remedy; a sound heart is the life of the flesh (Pro 14:30).
Hebrew chabash (H2280) — to bind up; he healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds (Psa 147:3).
Greek iaomai (G2390) — to heal, to cure; by whose stripes ye were healed (1Pe 2:24).
usage: “Rephaiah the son of Hur, the ruler of the half part of Jerusalem”.
“They were valiant men of might in their generations”.
“Heal me, O LORD, and I shall be healed” (Jer 17:14).

etymology: Hebrew Zerachyah (H2228), the LORD has risen or the LORD shines forth — from zarach (H2224), to rise as the sun, to break forth as light, and Yah, the covenant name.
biblical_def: Zerahiah stands in the high-priestly line of Aaron through Eleazar and Phinehas: Uzzi begat Zerahiah, and Zerahiah begat Meraioth (1Ch 6:6), and the genealogy is repeated in the descent of the sons of Aaron (1Ch 6:51). The same line is traced backward in Ezra's own pedigree, where the scribe establishes his right to the priesthood by naming his fathers up to Aaron — the son of Zerahiah, the son of Uzzi, the son of Bukki (Ezr 7:4). A second Zerahiah is the father of Elihoenai, who came up from Babylon with Ezra bringing two hundred males (Ezr 8:4). The name means the LORD has risen, from the verb Scripture uses of the sun coming up over the horizon, and the prophets turn it into a figure for the coming of God to His people: the LORD shall arise upon thee, and his glory shall be seen upon thee (Isa 60:2); unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings (Mal 4:2). A priestly house that carried such a name carried a promise it did not live to see fulfilled.
webster_summary: A priest in the high-priestly line of Aaron through Eleazar, named in Ezra's own pedigree; his name means the LORD has risen.
webster_full: ZERAHIAH, Hebrew Zerachyah, the LORD has risen, or the LORD shines forth.
1. A priest of the line of Eleazar the son of Aaron; son of Uzzi and father of Meraioth.
He stands in the pedigree by which Ezra proved his descent from Aaron.
2. Father of Elihoenai, who returned from Babylon with Ezra and two hundred males.
From zarach, to rise as the sun or break forth as light.
scriptures: And Uzzi begat Zerahiah, and Zerahiah begat Meraioth,
Bukki his son, Uzzi his son, Zerahiah his son,
Ezr 7:4
The son of Zerahiah, the son of Uzzi, the son of Bukki,
And Abishua begat Bukki, and Bukki begat Uzzi,
corruption_summary: Genealogies are dismissed as tedious padding; in Ezra's hands one is the legal proof of a right to minister.
corruption_paragraphs: The lists of begettings are the most skipped pages in the Bible, and the habit of skipping them costs the reader more than he knows. Ezra 7 shows what a genealogy is for. Before the historian tells us anything Ezra did, he lays out sixteen generations from Ezra back to Aaron the chief priest, because the whole authority of the reformation that follows rests on the man having a right to the office he exercised. The same book records the opposite case: priests who could not find their register were, as polluted, put from the priesthood (Ezr 2:62). Descent was not sentiment; it was law.

The New Testament keeps the principle while changing the register. Office in the church rests on a real call, tested and recognised: no man taketh this honour unto himself, but he that is called of God, as was Aaron (Heb 5:4); elders are to be examined against a written standard and appointed with laid-on hands, and let these also first be proved (1Ti 3:10). And the greatest genealogy of all opens the New Testament, because the claim that Jesus is the Christ depends on His descent from David and from Abraham. The principle to recover is that God works through documented, checkable, ordinary succession, and that a church too impatient to read a list will end up too impatient to verify a minister.
roots_summary: Hebrew Zerachyah (H2228), from zarach (H2224), to rise, to shine forth, with Yah.
roots_lines: Hebrew zarach (H2224) — to rise, to break forth as the sun; the sun ariseth (Ecc 1:5).
Hebrew Zerachyah (H2228) — a priest of Eleazar's line; 1 Chronicles 6:6, 6:51, Ezra 7:4, 8:4.
Hebrew zerach (H2225) — a rising, a dawning; the noun of the same root.
Hebrew yachas (H3187) — to reckon genealogically, to enrol; the machinery of Ezra 2 and 7.
Hebrew shemesh tsedaqah — the Sun of righteousness, who shall arise with healing in his wings (Mal 4:2).
usage: “Uzzi begat Zerahiah, and Zerahiah begat Meraioth”.
“The son of Zerahiah, the son of Uzzi, the son of Bukki” — in Ezra's pedigree.
“The Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings” (Mal 4:2).

etymology: Hebrew Uriel (H222), God is my light or flame of God — from ur (H217), flame, light, and El (H410), God.
biblical_def: Two men in Scripture bear this name. The first is a Kohathite Levite in the line of Tahath (1Ch 6:24), and he appears at a decisive moment: when David, having failed at his first attempt to bring up the ark because it was not carried according to the ordinance, gathered the Levites to do it rightly. Of the sons of Kohath; Uriel the chief, and his brethren an hundred and twenty (1Ch 15:5), and David called for Zadok and Abiathar the priests, and for the Levites, for Uriel, Asaiah, and Joel, Shemaiah, and Eliel, and Amminadab (1Ch 15:11), charging them to sanctify themselves because the LORD our God made a breach upon us, for that we sought him not after the due order (1Ch 15:13). The second Uriel is of Gibeah, the father of Michaiah who was mother of Abijah king of Judah (2Ch 13:2). The name means God is my light, which is worth holding beside the reason Uriel the Kohathite was summoned: the first attempt had been sincere, joyful, musical and wrong, and what corrected it was not more zeal but the written word about who should carry the ark.
webster_summary: A chief of the Kohathite Levites who helped bring up the ark after the due order, and the grandfather of Abijah king of Judah. It means God is my light.
webster_full: URIEL, Hebrew Uriel, God is my light, or flame of God.
1. A Levite of the sons of Kohath, in the line of Tahath.
Chief of the Kohathites, with an hundred and twenty of his brethren, at the bringing up of the ark.
David charged him and the priests to sanctify themselves and carry it after the due order.
2. Uriel of Gibeah, father of Michaiah the mother of Abijah king of Judah.
scriptures: Tahath his son, Uriel his son, Uzziah his son, and Shaul his son.
Of the sons of Kohath; Uriel the chief, and his brethren an hundred and twenty:
And David called for Zadok and Abiathar the priests, and for the Levites, for Uriel, Asaiah, and Joel, Shemaiah, and Eliel, and Amminadab,
He reigned three years in Jerusalem. His mother's name also was Michaiah the daughter of Uriel of Gibeah. And there was war between Abijah and Jeroboam.
corruption_summary: Sincerity is treated as sufficient in worship; the ark taught Israel that God appoints the manner as well as the object.
corruption_paragraphs: David's first attempt to bring up the ark had everything a modern congregation would recognise as worship: the whole nation, singing, harps and psalteries and timbrels and cymbals, a new cart, and a king dancing. It ended with a dead man beside the road, and David was displeased, and was afraid of God that day (1Ch 13:11-12). When he tried again he said plainly what had been wrong: we sought him not after the due order. The ark was to be borne on the shoulders of Levites, by staves, as the law prescribed, and no amount of sincerity replaced the instruction.

This is the whole ground of the regulative principle of worship, which the Reformed churches hold and this dictionary confesses: what God has commanded in His worship is required, and what He has not commanded is not ours to add. Nadab and Abihu offered strange fire which he commanded them not (Lev 10:1); Israel at Sinai meant to worship the LORD by the calf (Exo 32:5) and it was still idolatry; and the Lord Jesus quoted Isaiah against worship taught by the precepts of men (Mat 15:9). The principle to recover is that God is not honoured by the earnestness with which we do what He never asked, and that the remedy for disordered worship is not less enthusiasm but the text.
roots_summary: Hebrew Uriel (H222), from ur (H217), flame, light, with El (H410), God.
roots_lines: Hebrew ur (H217) — flame, light; the element also standing behind the Urim of the breastplate.
Hebrew Uriel (H222) — a Kohathite chief (1Ch 15:5, 15:11) and the grandfather of Abijah (2Ch 13:2).
Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment, ordinance, due order; we sought him not after the due order (1Ch 15:13).
Hebrew Qehath (H6955) — Kohath, the Levitical house charged with the ark and the holy vessels.
Hebrew or (H216) — light; the LORD is my light and my salvation (Psa 27:1).
usage: “Of the sons of Kohath; Uriel the chief, and his brethren an hundred and twenty”.
“David called for Zadok and Abiathar the priests, and for the Levites, for Uriel”.
“We sought him not after the due order” (1Ch 15:13).

etymology: Hebrew Yeremoth (H3406), elevations or heights — a plural form from rum (H7311), to be high, to be lifted up, to be exalted.
biblical_def: Jeremoth is borne by several men, most of them Levites and most of them keeping something. One is a son of Becher of Benjamin (1Ch 7:8); one a son of Beriah among the heads of the fathers of Benjamin (1Ch 8:14); one is a Merarite Levite of the sons of Mushi — the sons of Mushi; Mahli, and Eder, and Jeremoth, three (1Ch 23:23). Another leads the fifteenth of the twenty-four courses of singers whom David set apart for the service of song in the house of the LORD, each course numbering twelve (1Ch 25:22). Two more appear in Ezra's list of those who had taken strange wives and put them away (Ezr 10:26-27). The name means heights, from rum, to be lifted up. It is the verb of exaltation throughout the Psalms — Be thou exalted, O God, above the heavens (Psa 57:5) — and also the verb of the proud heart that Scripture warns against, for the same word describes both the LORD who is high above all nations and the man whose heart is lifted up to his own destruction.
webster_summary: The name of several men, chiefly Levites, including the leader of the fifteenth course of singers appointed by David. It means heights.
webster_full: JEREMOTH, Hebrew Yeremoth, elevations, heights; from rum, to be high.
1. A son of Becher, of the tribe of Benjamin.
2. A son of Beriah, among the heads of the fathers of Benjamin at Jerusalem.
3. A Levite of the sons of Mushi, of the house of Merari.
4. The leader of the fifteenth course of the singers in the house of the LORD, he, his sons and his brethren, twelve.
scriptures: The sons of Mushi; Mahli, and Eder, and Jeremoth, three.

And the sons of Tola; Uzzi, and Rephaiah, and Jeriel, and Jahmai, and Jibsam, and Shemuel, heads of their father's house, to wit, of Tola: they were valiant men of might in their generations; whose number was in the days of David two and twenty thousand and six hundred.
And of the sons of Elam; Mattaniah, Zechariah, and Jehiel, and Abdi, and Jeremoth, and Eliah.

Of Jeduthun: the sons of Jeduthun; Gedaliah, and Zeri, and Jeshaiah, Hashabiah, and Mattithiah, six, under the hands of their father Jeduthun, who prophesied with a harp, to give thanks and to praise the LORD.
corruption_summary: Music in worship is judged by its effect on the congregation; David ordered it as a ministry of the word, prophesying with harps.
corruption_paragraphs: The argument about music in the church is nearly always conducted as a question of taste and effect: what moves people, what draws them, what suits the culture. First Chronicles 25 approaches it from another direction entirely. David and the captains of the host separated the singers to their service, and the text describes what they were doing as prophesying — who prophesied with a harp, to give thanks and to praise the LORD (1Ch 25:3). The singers were ordered into twenty-four courses by lot, trained, numbered, and set under their fathers. It was an office, not an atmosphere.

Two things follow. First, the content governs: sung worship is the word of God returned to God, which is why Paul ties psalms, hymns and spiritual songs directly to the word of Christ dwell[ing] in you richly (Col 3:16). Second, the manner is ordered: trained men, appointed by name, in fixed courses, doing a set work. The principle to recover is that congregational song is a ministry of the word and is to be judged as preaching is judged — by whether what is sung is true, and whether the people are being taught by it — and not by how the room feels afterwards.
roots_summary: Hebrew Yeremoth (H3406), a plural from rum (H7311), to be high, to be exalted.
roots_lines: Hebrew rum (H7311) — to be high, to rise, to be exalted; Be thou exalted, O God, above the heavens (Psa 57:5).
Hebrew Yeremoth (H3406) — borne by Benjamites, Levites and singers; 1 Chronicles 7:8, 8:14, 23:23, 25:22.
Hebrew ramah (H7413) — a height, a high place; the same root, and the name of Samuel's town.
Hebrew naba (H5012) — to prophesy; used of the singers who prophesied with a harp (1Ch 25:3).
Greek psalmos (G5568) — a psalm, a song sung to accompaniment; psalms and hymns and spiritual songs (Col 3:16).
usage: “The sons of Mushi; Mahli, and Eder, and Jeremoth, three”.
“The fifteenth to Jeremoth, he, his sons, and his brethren, were twelve”.
“Who prophesied with a harp, to give thanks and to praise the LORD”.

etymology: Hebrew Yeshayah (H3470), the LORD has saved — from yasha (H3467), to save, to deliver, and Yah; the same Hebrew name the Authorized Version renders Isaiah for the prophet, and Jeshaiah or Jesaiah for these other men.
biblical_def: Several men bear this name, none of them the prophet. One is a son of Hananiah in the royal line of David after the captivity, spelled Jesaiah (1Ch 3:21). One is a son of Jeduthun, among the singers who prophesied with a harp, to give thanks and to praise the LORD, and leader of the eighth of the twenty-four courses (1Ch 25:3, 15). One is a Levite of the sons of Eliezer, in the line set over the treasures of the house of God (1Ch 26:25). One came up from Babylon with Ezra at the head of seventy males of the sons of Elam (Ezr 8:7), and another with the sons of Merari (Ezr 8:19). One more stands in a Benjamite pedigree of those who dwelt at Jerusalem (Neh 11:7). The name says the LORD has saved, in the perfect tense: not that He will, or may, but that He has. It is the same confession that the prophet Isaiah carried through sixty-six chapters and that reappears in Greek as the name given to Mary's son, for he shall save his people from their sins (Mat 1:21).
webster_summary: The name of several men — a descendant of David, a son of Jeduthun among the singers, a Levite, and two who returned with Ezra. It means the LORD has saved.
webster_full: JESHAIAH, Hebrew Yeshayah, the LORD has saved; the same name as Isaiah.
1. A son of Hananiah in the royal line of Judah after the captivity; written Jesaiah.
2. A son of Jeduthun, and leader of the eighth course of the singers.
3. A Levite of the sons of Eliezer, over the treasures of the house of God.
4. One who came up with Ezra at the head of seventy males of the sons of Elam.

corruption_summary: Salvation is spoken of as a process still to be completed; the name puts the decisive act in the perfect tense, already done.
corruption_paragraphs: Much popular religion keeps salvation permanently future and conditional — something a man hopes to obtain if he finishes well, so that assurance is presumption and the believer is meant to live in suspense. Scripture speaks in three tenses and refuses to collapse them. There is a past: by grace are ye saved through faith… it is the gift of God (Eph 2:8), and who hath saved us, and called us with an holy calling (2Ti 1:9). There is a present: unto us which are saved it is the power of God (1Co 1:18). And there is a future: now is our salvation nearer than when we believed (Rom 13:11).

The name Jeshaiah sits on the first of these, and it is the tense that grounds the others. Justification is a completed act of God, declaring the believer righteous once for all on the ground of Christ's imputed righteousness; sanctification is the lifelong work that follows; glorification is the certain end. To confuse the first with the second is to make a man's standing depend on his progress, which is the error the Reformation was fought over. The principle to recover is the order: because the LORD has saved, the believer may labour at holiness out of security rather than for it, and he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ (Php 1:6).
roots_summary: Hebrew Yeshayah (H3470), from yasha (H3467), to save, with Yah, the covenant name.

etymology: Hebrew Shima (H8092), report, fame, a thing heard — from shama (H8085), to hear; also written Shimma and Shammah.
biblical_def: Several men bear this name, and the most important is David's third brother, son of Jesse, written Shimma at 1 Chronicles 2:13 and Shammah in the account of Samuel's visit to Bethlehem. He is the brother who passed before Samuel and was not chosen; and his chief claim in the record belongs to his son. When the Philistine giants came out again in the later wars, when he defied Israel, Jonathan the son of Shimea David's brother slew him (1Ch 20:7). The uncle killed Goliath; the nephew killed another of the same breed a generation later. Two further men of the name are Levites: Shimea in the line of Merari (1Ch 6:30), and Shimea the father of Berachiah and grandfather of Asaph the singer, who stood on his right hand in the service of song (1Ch 6:39). A son of David born in Jerusalem also appears as Shimea in one list and Shammua in the others (1Ch 3:5). The name means a thing heard, a report or fame — fitting for a family whose name got about.
webster_summary: Chiefly the third son of Jesse, brother of David, whose son Jonathan slew a Philistine giant; also two Levites and a son of David.
webster_full: SHIMEA, Hebrew Shima, report, fame; also written Shimma and Shammah.
1. The third son of Jesse and elder brother of David.
His son Jonathan slew the Philistine giant who defied Israel.
2. A Levite of the house of Merari, son of Uzzah.
3. Father of Berachiah and grandfather of Asaph the singer. 4. A son of David born in Jerusalem.
scriptures: And Jesse begat his firstborn Eliab, and Abinadab the second, and Shimma the third,
But when he defied Israel, Jonathan the son of Shimea David's brother slew him.
Shimea his son, Haggiah his son, Asaiah his son.
And his brother Asaph, who stood on his right hand, even Asaph the son of Berachiah, the son of Shimea,
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the brother passed over at the anointing still had a place in the story.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Shimea attracts no controversy. His position does press a question that troubles many a believer: what becomes of the one who was not chosen. Seven sons of Jesse passed before Samuel and were refused, Shimea among them, and the youngest was anointed instead. Scripture does not soften that scene. It records the LORD's reason — man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart (1Sa 16:7) — and moves on.

What it also records, quietly and much later, is that Shimea's son killed a giant. The brother who was not made king fathered a man who fought the same enemy his uncle had fought, and Chronicles gives him the credit by name. Every member of the body has a function, and God hath set the members every one of them in the body, as it hath pleased him (1Co 12:18). The principle to recover is that not being chosen for one office is not being passed over by God; the calling that did not come to Shimea came to his son, and the household that raised that son had done real work in the kingdom.

etymology: Hebrew Buqqi (H1231), commonly read wasting or proved of the LORD, a shortened form of Bukkiah; from a root signifying to empty out or to lay waste.
biblical_def: Two men bear this name. The first is the prince of the tribe of Dan appointed by the LORD to help divide the land of Canaan among the tribes: the prince of the tribe of the children of Dan, Bukki the son of Jogli (Num 34:22). That commission is worth weighing. God named ten tribal princes, with Eleazar the priest and Joshua, to apportion an inheritance that had been promised to Abraham four hundred years before and that none of them had yet possessed. The second Bukki is a priest in the high-priestly line of Aaron — Abishua begat Bukki, and Bukki begat Uzzi (1Ch 6:5, 51) — and he stands in the pedigree by which Ezra proved his descent from Aaron (Ezr 7:4). The name is a plain one and the men are obscure, but between them they hold the two great institutions of Israel: the land and the priesthood. One divided the inheritance; the other carried the line that ministered in it.
webster_summary: The prince of the tribe of Dan appointed to divide the land, and a priest in the high-priestly line of Aaron named in Ezra's pedigree.
webster_full: BUKKI, Hebrew Buqqi, commonly read wasting, or proved of the LORD.
1. The son of Jogli, prince of the tribe of the children of Dan.
He was named by the LORD to divide the land of Canaan for an inheritance.
2. A priest of the line of Eleazar; son of Abishua and father of Uzzi.
He stands in the pedigree by which Ezra proved his descent from Aaron.
scriptures: And the prince of the tribe of the children of Dan, Bukki the son of Jogli.
And Abishua begat Bukki, and Bukki begat Uzzi,
Bukki his son, Uzzi his son, Zerahiah his son,
Ezr 7:4
The son of Zerahiah, the son of Uzzi, the son of Bukki,
corruption_summary: Inheritance is treated as what a man accumulates; in Scripture it is what God allots, and the allotting was done before the land was held.
corruption_paragraphs: Numbers 34 has God appointing men by name to divide a country Israel had not yet entered, and drawing its borders in advance. The whole procedure assumes something the modern mind resists: that the portion is given rather than seized, and that the distribution belongs to God. Joshua later carried it out by lot (Jos 14:2), which removed human preference from the process altogether — the lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD (Pro 16:33).

The New Testament keeps the vocabulary and raises the stakes. Believers have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will (Eph 1:11); the Spirit is the earnest of that inheritance; and it is incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven (1Pe 1:4). The principle to recover is contentment with an allotted portion. The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage (Psa 16:6) is the settled word of a man who believed his lot was measured out by a Father, and it is the cure for the restless comparison that eats up so much Christian life.

etymology: Hebrew Elasah (H501), God has made — from El (H410), God, and asah (H6213), to do, to make, to accomplish; the verb of the six days of creation.
biblical_def: Two men in Chronicles bear this name. The first is of Judah, in the line of Jerahmeel: Azariah begat Helez, and Helez begat Eleasah (1Ch 2:39). The second is a Benjamite of the house of Saul, four generations down from Jonathan through Mephibosheth and Micah — Rapha was his son, Eleasah his son, Azel his son (1Ch 8:37; 9:43). That second line deserves notice. Saul's house fell at Gilboa and his surviving grandson was a lame man eating at David's table; yet Chronicles traces the family on, generation by generation, for centuries, and Eleasah is one of the links. A third man, spelled Elasah, was one of the two Zedekiah sent to Babylon and by whose hand Jeremiah sent his letter to the captives (Jer 29:3) — the letter that told them to build houses and plant gardens and seek the peace of the city. The name means God has made, from asah, and it is a fitting name for links in a chain: the houses of Israel continued because God kept making them continue.
webster_summary: The name of men in the genealogies of Judah and of the house of Saul; a third, spelled Elasah, carried Jeremiah's letter to the exiles.
webster_full: ELEASAH, Hebrew Elasah, God has made.
1. A man of Judah in the line of Jerahmeel, son of Helez.
2. A Benjamite of the house of Saul, descended from Jonathan through Mephibosheth.
His son was Azel, who had six sons whose names are recorded.
3. Elasah the son of Shaphan, sent by Zedekiah to Babylon, who carried Jeremiah's letter to the captives.
scriptures: And Azariah begat Helez, and Helez begat Eleasah,
And Moza begat Binea: Rapha was his son, Eleasah his son, Azel his son:
And Moza begat Binea; and Rephaiah his son, Eleasah his son, Azel his son.
Jer 29:3
By the hand of Elasah the son of Shaphan, and Gemariah the son of Hilkiah, (whom Zedekiah king of Judah sent unto Babylon to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon) saying,
corruption_summary: A fallen house is assumed to be finished; Chronicles keeps tracing Saul's line for centuries after Gilboa.
corruption_paragraphs: Saul's story ends in disaster: rejected as king, dead by his own sword on Gilboa with three of his sons, his head fastened in the temple of Dagon. Everything about the narrative says the house is over. Then Chronicles, writing centuries later, walks the family forward name by name — Jonathan, Merib-baal, Micah, Ahaz, Jehoadah, Alemeth, Azmaveth, Zimri, Moza, Binea, Rapha, Eleasah, Azel — and gives Azel's six sons by name. A house under judgment was still a house, and God kept a record of it.

The mercy in this is not that Saul was excused; Scripture never excuses him. It is that judgment on a man is not annihilation of his line, and that God's dealings with a family are longer and more patient than one generation's catastrophe. David had sworn to Jonathan that he would not cut off his kindness from his house for ever (1Sa 20:15), and the register in Chronicles is that oath still being kept long after both men were dust. The principle to recover is that no believer should write off a family — his own included — on the evidence of its worst generation. He hath not dealt with us after our sins; nor rewarded us according to our iniquities (Psa 103:10).
